prompt.context: Our client is a large Chinese conglomerate with a lot of cash on its hands. They decided to invest this money in a plant that, by the end of this year, will have a full production capacity of 8 million aluminum wheels annually. Management assumes that it will be able to sell 20% of its production in the domestic Chinese market.
prompt.question: The company hired Roland Berger to determine if it can sell the remaining 80% of its production to the US market, which is the largest vehicle market in the world. What do you think?

clarifying_info.q: How many vehicles are produced in the US each year?
clarifying_info.a: About 17 million vehicles are produced in the US each year.

clarifying_info.q: What share of US vehicles have aluminum wheels?
clarifying_info.a: About 70% of new US vehicles are equipped with aluminum wheels.

clarifying_info.q: What is the size of the after-market for aluminum wheels?
clarifying_info.a: There are about 85 million cars in the after-market, but only about 24 million are less than 5 years old. About 10% of used car owners whose cars are less than 5 years old buy aluminum wheels.

clarifying_info.q: How do OEMs select their aluminum wheel suppliers?
clarifying_info.a: Most companies will select one supplier who will supply the aluminum wheels for the entire lifetime of a car model. Suppliers are usually selected 24 months before a new model goes into production and have stringent quality controls.

clarifying_info.q: Is expanding to markets outside the US an option?
clarifying_info.a: The client thought about that as another option, but they would really like to work with just the US.

framework: 1. Quantify the client's US target: calculate wheels and equivalent cars from 80% of 8M production
2. Size the US new car aluminum wheel market: units × aluminum penetration rate
3. Size the US after-market aluminum wheel market: eligible cars × replacement rate
4. Compare client's target supply to both markets to determine required market share
5. Assess feasibility of OEM channel: supplier selection process, lead times, quality requirements
6. Assess feasibility of after-market channel: fragmentation and share required
7. Identify alternative entry route: sub-contracting capacity to existing US OEM suppliers
8. Recommendation: most viable path forward and key risks

questions.prompt: How many aluminum wheels does the client need to sell in the US, and how many cars does that represent?
questions.guidance: Total capacity = 8M wheels/year. Domestic sales = 20% = 1.6M wheels. US target = 80% = 6.4M wheels = 1.6M cars (at 4 wheels per car, excluding spare).

math.setup: Total capacity: 8,000,000 wheels. US target = 80% of 8M. Cars = wheels / 4.
math.answer: 6.4 million wheels, equivalent to 1.6 million cars

questions.prompt: How large is the US new car aluminum wheel market? What market share would the client need to capture?
questions.guidance: 17M new vehicles × 70% aluminum penetration = ~12M new cars with aluminum wheels = ~48M wheels/year. Client needs 6.4M wheels → about 13% share of the OEM market. While the share sounds achievable, the supplier selection process (24+ months lead time, stringent quality) makes rapid entry very difficult.

math.setup: New US vehicles per year × aluminum penetration rate = addressable new car market.
math.answer: ~12M cars, ~48M wheels; client would need ~13% OEM share

questions.prompt: How large is the US after-market for aluminum wheels? What share would the client need?
questions.guidance: 85M after-market cars, 24M less than 5 years old, 10% of those owners buy aluminum wheels = 2.4M sets/year = 9.6M wheels/year. Client needs 6.4M wheels → ~67% after-market share. This is unrealistically high for a fragmented market with no brand presence.

math.setup: After-market eligible cars × purchase rate = annual after-market demand.
math.answer: ~2.4M sets (~9.6M wheels); client would need ~67% after-market share — unrealistic

questions.prompt: Given the OEM supplier selection process, can the client realistically win OEM contracts by year-end?
questions.guidance: Suppliers are selected 24 months before a new model goes into production. Getting onto a preferred supplier list likely requires another 12 months of qualification, for a total lead time of ~3 years. Since the plant is ready this year, there is not enough time to win OEM business before full capacity is online. The OEM channel is not viable in the near term.

questions.prompt: What alternative market entry route might allow the client to sell at scale in the US despite these barriers?
questions.guidance: The client could sub-contract production capacity to existing US OEM suppliers. Because the client can likely produce at lower cost in China, it becomes a manufacturing partner for suppliers who already hold OEM contracts. This sacrifices some margin (the intermediary captures a spread) but allows rapid large-scale entry into the US market without needing to win OEM contracts directly or capture an unrealistic share of the fragmented after-market.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors should the client consider when deciding how to enter the US aluminum wheel market?

categories.name: Market Access & Channels
ideas: Direct OEM supplier contracts (requires 24–36 month qualification lead time)
After-market retail distribution (fragmented, 67% share needed — not viable alone)
Sub-contracting to existing OEM suppliers (fastest large-scale route)
Acquire or JV with an existing US supplier to inherit contracts and relationships

categories.name: Competitive Positioning
ideas: Cost advantage from Chinese manufacturing
Quality certification requirements (ISO/TS, OEM-specific audits)
Brand recognition: unknown in US market
Ability to meet OEM stringent quality and delivery standards

categories.name: Regulatory & Trade
ideas: Import tariffs on automotive components
US content requirements for certain OEM programs
Safety and certification standards (DOT, SAE)
Trade policy risk / anti-dumping duties

categories.name: Operational Considerations
ideas: Logistics cost and lead time from China to US
Inventory buffering requirements for just-in-time OEM supply
Currency risk (RMB vs USD)
Capacity utilization if US contracts are delayed

categories.name: Strategic Alternatives
ideas: Diversify beyond US to European or other markets
Focus on after-market with aggressive pricing and marketing investment
License technology to a US manufacturer
Use US entry as a stepping stone to build brand before pursuing OEM contracts

recommendation: Sub-contracting production capacity to existing US OEM wheel suppliers is the most viable near-term entry route, given the 3-year OEM qualification lead time and the impractical 67% share required to serve the after-market alone.
The client should approach top US aluminum wheel suppliers, offering lower-cost contract manufacturing, accepting a lower margin in exchange for rapid volume and market presence.
risks: Margin compression from intermediary markup — sub-contracting is less profitable than direct OEM or retail sales
Dependence on a single distribution partner creates negotiation risk
Quality or delivery failures could damage reputation before the client builds its own US brand
Trade policy shifts (tariffs, anti-dumping) could erode the cost advantage
next_steps: Identify the top 3–5 US aluminum wheel suppliers as potential sub-contracting partners and initiate outreach
Obtain relevant quality certifications (ISO/TS 16949 or IATF 16949) to meet OEM standards
Develop a 3-year roadmap to qualify as a direct OEM supplier while sub-contracting generates revenue in the interim
Monitor US trade policy for tariff risk and evaluate hedging options
